title: Life of the party: Democrats and the search for a post-Trump future – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: ECFR sorts 2026 midterm Democrats into three camps — revolutionaries (system is unjust), renovators (system is corrupted) and revivalists (MAGA broke bipartisanship) — whose domestic diagnoses predict their foreign policy on trade, force, China, Israel and Europe; whichever wins, a post-Trump Democratic foreign policy will be far less transatlanticist, with hardened burden-sharing expectations and Europe barely on the agenda.

insights.claim: A Democratic majority in one or both chambers after the November 2026 midterms looks likely, but it will do little to constrain Trump's foreign policy because the administration routes around Congress; little will change until the White House occupant does.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Do not price a midterm-driven reversal of tariffs or foreign policy; policy regime shift is a 2029 event at earliest.
insights.quote: little will change until the occupant of the White House does
insights.locator: Europeans hoping that a midterm victory

insights.claim: Trump's administration announced sweeping 10% baseline tariffs on 80 countries in summer 2026, while the US was four months into a war with Iran.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Baseline-tariff regime and Iran war are the live macro backdrop for 2026 trade and energy risk.
insights.locator: This summer, the FIFA World Cup

insights.claim: The ideological battle between Democratic camps will matter more than House or Senate arithmetic over the next two years because one camp will set the party's agenda for the 2028 presidential race.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Track which camp wins primaries and 2028 positioning to forecast post-2029 US trade, defence and tech policy.
insights.quote: The ideological battles between Democrats will matter more than the arithmetic of the Senate or the House
insights.locator: The ideological battles between Democrats

insights.claim: If Democrats win the midterms, the next two years will see Trump weak and Democrats not yet strong, with no policy ideas coming from Washington on future collaboration with Europe.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Expect a two-year US policy vacuum on transatlantic initiatives; European-led proposals will set the agenda.
insights.quote: the next two years will see Trump weak and the Democrats not yet strong
insights.locator: As Democrats are not paying any attention

insights.claim: Democrats cluster into three ideal-type camps: revolutionaries (the system is unjust by design and needs structural change), renovators (the system has been corrupted by money and captured interests and needs reform) and revivalists (Trump/MAGA polarisation broke a working bipartisan system).
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: A usable lens to map any Democratic candidate's likely policy on trade, defence, China and tech regulation.
insights.locator: The revolutionaries argue that the political

insights.claim: Sorting candidates by their diagnosis of what went wrong in America reliably predicts how they discuss domestic and global problems, based on analysis of dozens of 2026 Democratic primary and general campaigns.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Candidate rhetoric about root causes is a leading indicator of their foreign-policy stance.
insights.locator: The revolutionaries, renovators and revivalists are ideal types

insights.claim: Revolutionaries' signature proposals include nationalising big corporations, adding Supreme Court seats, congressional term limits, campaign-finance overhaul and higher taxes on the ultra-wealthy, alongside Medicare for All.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: A revolutionary-led party implies material tail risk for large-cap corporates, healthcare insurers and top-bracket tax rates.
insights.locator: Because the revolutionaries diagnose the political system

insights.claim: Revolutionaries see the military-industrial complex as America's de facto industrial policy and aim to cut defence spending, ban corporate PAC spending to reduce the influence of defence contractors and AIPAC, and redirect money to diplomacy and domestic needs.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Revolutionary ascendancy is a direct negative for US defence-prime budgets.
insights.quote: The military-industrial complex doesn’t just enrich arms manufacturers—it has become our de facto industrial policy

insights.claim: Renovators overlap with revolutionaries on congressional stock-trading bans, term limits and campaign-finance reform but would reform rather than abolish agencies like ICE and treat the Democratic party as a vehicle worth steering.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Congressional stock-trading bans have cross-camp support and are a plausible near-term reform.
insights.locator: Because renovators share the same anger

insights.claim: Revivalists are the largest cross-section of the party, stand closest to party leadership, treat experience as a credential and centre their pitch on defeating Trump and restoring bipartisan norms.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Revivalists remain the default establishment scenario for a Democratic policy restoration.
insights.locator: Revivalists comprise the largest cross-section

insights.claim: Primary results so far are mixed: revolutionary firebrands such as Abdul El-Sayed and Angie Nixon won upset victories, renovators Jon Ossoff and James Talarico are running strong campaigns, and revivalists fare strongly across the board.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: No camp has won yet; keep scenario weights spread across all three for 2028 policy.
insights.locator: It is too early to know which

themes.theme: Trade: specific tariffs vs all tariffs

insights.claim: Affordability has defined the 2026 Democratic cycle since Zohran Mamdani's November 2025 New York mayoral win, and Democrats frame trade as 'affordability gone global', attacking Trump's tariffs as raising prices.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Cost-of-living messaging dominates; expect Democratic trade proposals framed around consumer prices.
insights.locator: In terms of foreign policy, trade

insights.claim: Democratic opposition to Trump's tariffs is an objection to these specific tariffs, not to tariffs in general; revolutionaries see small strategic tariffs as legitimate job-protection tools and call NAFTA a failure.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Don't assume a Democratic White House means a return to free trade — protectionism persists in modified form.
insights.quote: this consensus is an objection to these specific tariffs, not to all tariffs
insights.locator: In terms of foreign policy, trade

insights.claim: Renovators want to improve trade agreements, e.g. Jon Ossoff urged using the USMCA review to police Mexican labour and environmental practices; revivalists want to 'strengthen and renew' USMCA and limit tariffs and export controls to national-security uses akin to Biden's 'small-yard, high-fence'.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: USMCA review outcome and labour-standard enforcement are key variables for Mexico-exposed manufacturing and agriculture.
insights.locator: Renovators, on the other hand

insights.claim: International trade is no longer taken as an unqualified good within the Democratic party, and the American left is not returning to the internationalism of the 2010s.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Structural, bipartisan drift away from free trade argues for durable tariff/industrial-policy regimes beyond Trump.
insights.quote: The American left is not returning to the internationalism of the 2010s
insights.locator: One thing is for certain

insights.claim: Revivalists treat China as the defining national-security issue and view AI, space and weapons development as an arms race the US must win, with export controls, EV import controls, sanctions on CCP officials and TikTok bans all on the table.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Revivalist win implies continuity of hawkish export controls and Chinese-EV exclusion.
insights.locator: At the other end, revivalists treat China

insights.claim: Revolutionaries would rather limit AI development to protect jobs, workers and the environment than accelerate AI to compete with China, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez declined to commit US troops to defend Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: A revolutionary-led party is a regulatory risk for frontier AI and a softer Taiwan deterrence signal.
insights.locator: This camp’s scepticism of the use of force

insights.claim: Renovators would require data centres to be energy- and water-self-sufficient or even back moratoriums on data centres, even at the expense of frontier model development.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Data-centre moratorium/self-sufficiency rules are a policy risk for hyperscaler capex and data-centre REITs under a renovator-influenced Democratic government.
insights.quote: call for moratoriums on data centres, even if that threatens frontier model development
insights.locator: Renovators sit in the middle

insights.claim: Strategic competition with China is no longer the Democratic modus operandi as it was under Biden.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Possible softening of China hawkishness post-Trump would matter for export-control-exposed semiconductor names.
insights.locator: One thing is for certain

insights.claim: Nearly every Democrat criticised Trump's Iran war and many voiced reservations about the Venezuela operation that removed Nicolás Maduro; renovators frame both as corruption, alleging the Venezuela operation served oil executives and donors.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Democratic scrutiny of oil-sector gains from Venezuela could become an investigative risk for US oil majors after the midterms.
insights.locator: America’s two latest military operations

insights.claim: Israel policy splits the camps most cleanly: revolutionaries want a full arms embargo including defensive systems, renovators would ban offensive weapons sales while supporting defensive systems, and revivalists treat arms sales case by case while blaming Netanyahu.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Direction of the Democratic party on Israel arms sales is a medium-term risk for US defence exporters' Israel business.
insights.locator: Israel is where the three camps separate

insights.claim: Revolutionary candidates have unseated incumbents on Israel-arms positions, e.g. Melat Kiros beat nearly 30-year incumbent Diana DeGette and Darializa Avila Chevalier beat Adriano Espaillat.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Evidence that the arms-embargo position is electorally viable in Democratic primaries.
insights.locator: This distinction has already defined

insights.claim: On Russia sanctions, renovators Chris Murphy and Jon Ossoff were sceptical of the Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026, which would authorise tariffs up to 100% on the top-five foreign buyers of Russian energy, while revivalists Mark Kelly and Ruben Gallego backed it.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Secondary-tariff threats on Russian-energy buyers (e.g. large Asian importers) retain bipartisan support among revivalists.
insights.locator: Those in the renovator and revivalist camps

insights.claim: 2026 midterm Democratic candidates barely mention Europe, Russia or Ukraine; Europe was hardly mentioned in TV interviews, stump speeches or posts on X, as debates focus on China, Iran, Israel and Venezuela.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Transatlantic security guarantees will not regain priority under a Democratic administration; supports structural European defence spending.
insights.locator: As Europeans navigate the new American left

insights.claim: Whichever camp prevails, Democratic foreign policy will be a far cry from past transatlanticism: burden-sharing expectations will have hardened and attachment to the Atlantic alliance faded, with younger Democrats viewing alliances through effectiveness and narrow shared interests.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: European rearmament is a multi-administration trend, not a Trump-era blip — supportive for European defence equities.
insights.quote: Many Democrats no longer see the transatlantic relationship as an inheritance that they have a duty to preserve
insights.locator: Many Democrats no longer see

insights.claim: Revivalists credit European allies with committing 5% of GDP to military spending and treat burden-sharing as settled, but even they are unlikely to restore the old transatlantic division of labour.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: The 5% NATO spending commitment is the baseline even in the most pro-alliance Democratic scenario.
insights.locator: Revivalists remain the most attached

insights.claim: Revolutionaries accept or even welcome European strategic autonomy and are least likely to campaign for returning US troops that Trump withdraws from Europe, while opposing a Europe defined by militarisation and austerity.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: US troop drawdowns from Europe are unlikely to be reversed under a revolutionary-led party.
insights.locator: Revolutionaries are interested in a transatlantic relationship

insights.claim: Democrats across camps increasingly view European leaders who curried Trump's favour as part of the problem — enablers of oligarchy, corruption or a global bully.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: European appeasement of Trump carries a future relationship cost with a Democratic administration.
insights.quote: who would like to see in Europeans a standard-bearer and not an enabler
insights.locator: When they do pay attention to Europe

insights.claim: Even under Biden, the Inflation Reduction Act, the Afghanistan withdrawal and AUKUS showed a US pursuing objectives unilaterally with limited European consultation.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Expect future Democratic industrial policy to also discriminate against European firms, as the IRA did.
insights.locator: Europeans’ experience of the Biden administration

insights.claim: ECFR recommends Europe propose a cross-camp 'fair trade' agenda combining openness with labour protections, coordinated responses to Chinese industrial overcapacity, minimum wage requirements and climate standards, moving away from indiscriminate tariffs and negotiated exemptions.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: A labour/climate-standards-based trade framework could become the next transatlantic trade architecture, relevant for carbon-intensive and low-wage import competitors.
insights.locator: A “fair trade” agenda that combines

insights.claim: A joint transatlantic AI framework on consumer protection, fair taxation of digital platforms and open AI access for public goods would appeal most to renovators, with France and Britain (G7 host in 2028) suggested as convenors.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: Digital-platform taxation and AI regulation may gain US Democratic allies — a regulatory headwind for big tech.
insights.locator: A joint framework for AI

insights.claim: All three camps would favour a rebalanced NATO in which Europeans take on more force generation, command structures and regional deterrence, allowing a smaller US military footprint.
insights.speaker: Célia Belin, Chris Herrmann, Nevada Joan Lee
insights.so_what: European force-generation build-out implies sustained procurement demand across European defence industry.
